Lesson 01

Fine-tune only after a measured failure of the cheaper fixes

Why it matters

Prompt, schema, retrieval, and tools come first. Training is for a gap those did not close.

Try it: Prompt, retrieval, or fine-tune

Lesson
01 of 06
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Order

Train
Only for the leftover gap

Compare to the base

Fine-tuning changes the model's weights, usually by training on examples of the behavior you want. It costs data work, compute, and a new model you have to host and re-eval. It is the right tool when the base model already has the facts — or you will keep retrieving the facts — and still will not hold a format, a style, or a domain decision that you can show in examples.

Do not fine-tune to

  • Memorize a handbook that changes monthly. Retrieve it.
  • Hide a secret or a policy the prompt already states and the eval already passes.
  • Repair a broken tool. Fix the tool.
  • Chase a leaderboard with no task of your own.

The decision record is the eval from School 09 plus a sentence: which failures remain, and why a prompt or a retrieval change cannot address them. If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to train.

Practice

Write that decision sentence for a real or fictional system. 'Not yet, because …' is a complete answer.

Check

Name one problem retrieval solves better than fine-tuning.

Show the answer

Facts that change, or facts that must be cited from a source you can update without training.

Lesson 02

LoRA trains a small adapter and leaves the base model frozen

Why it matters

QLoRA does the same while the frozen base is stored in a quantized form.

Try it: LoRA rank

Lesson
02 of 06
Time
13 min
Level
Core
Train
Small matrices
Freeze
The base
QLoRA
Quantized base, same adapter idea

Full fine-tuning updates every weight. That is expensive and easy to damage. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes the base model and trains small matrices that sit alongside certain layers. You store the adapter, not a full second copy of the model. At inference you load the base plus the adapter.

QLoRA quantizes that frozen base so the training job fits on a smaller GPU. The adapter is still what you train. People say 'I quantized' when they mean 'I fine-tuned' and the reverse. In a design review, say which one you did.

Preference methods such as DPO train from pairs of better and worse answers. They are a fit when the issue is which output a person prefers, and a poor fit when the issue is a missing document. You still need a base that can produce the better answer often enough to learn from.

Tools you will see named

Hugging Face PEFT, Axolotl, Unsloth, and the hosted fine-tuning APIs from the major labs. The method matters more than the brand: frozen base, small adapter, same eval before and after.

Practice

In three sentences, explain to a teammate the difference between quantizing a model to run it and training a LoRA adapter on it.

Check

What do you save after a LoRA run?

Show the answer

The adapter, and a record of the base model id it attaches to. The adapter without the matching base is not a model.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

Loss sketch

A sketch of a shape you will see in training write-ups. Training loss falls. Validation loss can rise when the run memorizes. This is not a log from a named model.

Lesson 03

Training data has a format, a license, and a leakage problem

Why it matters

Examples teach the behavior. They also teach secrets you forgot were in the log.

Try it: Prompt, retrieval, or fine-tune

Lesson
03 of 06
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Examples
Teach the behavior
Also teach
Secrets left in the log
Split
Train is not the test

A typical supervised set is a list of conversations or instruction pairs: the input the model will see, and the output you want. The format must match how you will call the model later. Training on essays and then calling the model as a JSON API is a self-inflicted miss.

  • You need the right to train on every row. A model license, a website's terms, and your employer's policy can each forbid it.
  • Remove secrets, tokens, and personal data. A model that memorizes a key is a leak you cannot easily grep.
  • Remove exact copies of your eval tasks. If the eval is in the training set, the score is a memory test.
  • Include refusal and 'not in the source' examples if that is the behavior you want. A set of only happy paths teaches invention.
  • Keep a validation split that you do not train on.

Synthetic data

Data a model wrote is allowed only if you review it and you are allowed to use it. It repeats the teacher's mistakes at scale. A person still owns the guidelines.

Practice

Describe the columns of a training row for one task. Add a column for the source of the row and a yes/no for 'contains personal data'. That yes/no must be no before the row is usable.

Check

Why must eval tasks stay out of the training set?

Show the answer

Because a high score would then mean the model saw the answers, not that it generalized.

Lesson 04

Compare the adapter to the base model on the same tasks

Why it matters

Keep the adapter only if the scorecard says so, including the tasks that used to pass.

Try it: LoRA rank

Level
Practice

Run the School 09 tasks twice: base model, then base plus adapter. Same prompts, same retrieval, same tools. The adapter wins only if the failures you trained for improved and the safety tasks did not get worse.

Watch for a model that learned the training phrasing and now refuses to answer a valid variant. That shows up as regressions on tasks that used to pass. It is the usual cost of a small, narrow set.

  • Record the base id and the adapter id together.
  • If you quantize after training, eval the quantized result, not the pre-quantized one you will not ship.
  • If the adapter ties the base, do not ship it. You would be adding an artifact to host for no gain.

Practice

Write the comparison header: task, base result, adapter result, regression yes/no. Fill it with the decision you expect, and note which safety task would make you throw the adapter away.

Check

A adapter raises the average and fails a refusal task the base passed. Do you ship it?

Show the answer

No, if refusal is in the gate. An average can rise while a safety regression lands.

Lesson 05

Prefer a prompt or a tool when that is the whole gap

Why it matters

Most 'we should fine-tune' reviews end with a schema, a retrieval fix, or a smaller model.

Try it: Prompt, retrieval, or fine-tune

Lesson
05 of 06
Time
8 min
Level
Practice
Usual end
Schema, retrieval, or a smaller model
Train for
A pattern the index will not hold
Do not train
Facts you can update

Walk this list before you spend on training.

  1. The output shape is underspecified. Fix the schema.
  2. The fact is missing from the context. Fix retrieval or the tool.
  3. The fact is in the context and ignored. Fix placement, chunking, or the instruction to cite.
  4. A cheaper model fails and a larger base model passes. Use the larger model, or route only the hard rows.
  5. Only the remaining rows, with a stable behavior you can exemplify, are training candidates.

This is the judgment hiring panels are probing when they ask 'how do you decide to fine-tune'. The answer is a sequence of measured exclusions, not enthusiasm for training.

Practice

Take the decision sentence from 10-01 and run it down this list. Stop at the first item that applies.

Check

When is a larger base model a better answer than a fine-tune?

Show the answer

When the larger model already passes the same tasks and you can afford it. You have not found a behavior the base cannot learn from context.

This room says when that copy is the wrong tool, what LoRA and QLoRA actually freeze, how distillation differs from a preference loss, and the eval gate that is allowed to stop the run.</p><h3>01Executive summary</h3><ul><li>LoRA, in Hu et al., freezes the pretrained weights and trains a low-rank update. Their GPT-3 175B comparison claims about 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters and about 3 times less GPU memory than full Adam fine-tuning, and they say the update can be merged so inference latency does not grow. Those figures are the paper’s, historical. [cite:1]</li><li>QLoRA, in Dettmers et al., backpropagates into LoRA adapters through a frozen 4-bit model. They report finetuning a 65B model on one 48GB GPU, against a 16-bit figure they put above 780GB. NF4, double quantization, and paged optimizers are their three memory ideas. Guanaco’s Vicuna scores are historical. [cite:2]</li><li>Distillation, in Hinton, Vinyals, and Dean, transfers a mapping from a cumbersome model or ensemble into a smaller model you can deploy. The relative probabilities of wrong answers are part of what they say the student should learn. It is not a synonym for LoRA. [cite:3]</li><li>DPO, in Rafailov et al., rewrites the RLHF objective so a classification loss recovers the optimal policy. They say you do not sample from the language model during that fine-tune and you do not run a separate reinforcement-learning loop. Their sentiment and summarization results are historical. [cite:4]</li><li>NIST’s Measure function says to test before deployment and regularly in operation. A fine-tune that skips the golden set from T5 has not been measured. OWASP LLM04:2025 names poisoning of fine-tuning data as its own risk. [cite:5] [cite:6]</li></ul><aside class="callout note"><h3>Why it matters for the lab engineer</h3><p>Contact-center teams reach for a fine-tune when a prompt sounds stiff or a bot misses a phrase. The failure is often a missing article, a missing tool, or a missing abstention. A weight update will memorize the calls you happened to export, including the wrong credit. This room is the gate: prompt and retriever first, adapters only when the eval says the weights are the bug, and a smaller distilled model only when the teacher already passes the same cases.</p></aside><h3>02Architecture</h3><p>A run is data, a frozen base, a small update, and a gate. The gate can say no.</p><p>Diagram: Seven stages: cases, data, base, adapter, train, eval, ship or stop</p><ul><li>1 is the golden set from T5. It is not the training file.</li><li>2–4 are the update. LoRA and QLoRA keep the base frozen.</li><li>6 compares the adapter to the prompt baseline. 7 ships only on a pass.</li></ul><p>Sequence: the eval owner can stop the merge.</p><p>Diagram: Owner, data, trainer, base model, eval runner</p><p>The picture is a supervised or preference update on a frozen base. Distillation uses the same boxes with a teacher in the data step: the student trains on the teacher’s outputs, not on a new policy you invented in a spreadsheet. Nothing in the picture is a Control Hub menu. The phone system still routes the call after you ship.</p><h3>03Deep dive</h3><p>Fine-tuning changes weights so the next-token distribution moves toward the pairs you showed it. Prompting, from T2, changes the string inside the window. Retrieval, from T3, changes which documents are in that string. Tools, from T4, change the world and then put a result back in the string. If the fact is missing, a gradient will not fetch it. If the fact is in a PDF that changes every Tuesday, a fine-tune on last month’s PDF is a stale copy with extra confidence.</p><h3>Which failure gets which tool</h3><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Symptom</th><th>First tool</th><th>Weight update only if</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>The answer needs a fact that changes</td><td>Retrieve it, or call a tool. T3 and T4.</td><td>Never as the source of that fact. The weights will lag the PDF.</td></tr><tr><td>The shape is wrong and the fact is present</td><td>A few-shot example, in Brown’s sense: text, no gradient. [cite:7]</td><td>The golden set still misses the shape after the example, and you can name the pairs.</td></tr><tr><td>The model is right and too slow or too expensive</td><td>A smaller model, possibly distilled from a teacher that already passes. [cite:3]</td><td>You are not “teaching” a new policy. You are compressing one that passed.</td></tr><tr><td>You want a style or a ranking of answers</td><td>A preference set, and a method you can explain. DPO is one historical method. [cite:4]</td><td>The preference labels are not the test set, and a human can audit a sample.</td></tr><tr><td>A retrieved page talks the bot out of a cap</td><td>The tool enforces the cap. OWASP says fine-tuning does not fully mitigate injection. [cite:6]</td><td>You do not fine-tune “harder” and call the cap fixed.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><aside class="callout note"><h3>Gotcha</h3><p>A fine-tune on transcripts will imitate the agent who promised the credit, not the policy the agent violated. QLoRA’s own analysis says data quality mattered more than dataset size on their chatbot study. A 9k set beat a much larger set in that paper. Historical, and still the right warning: more rows of the wrong calls make a worse bot. [cite:2]</p></aside><h3>LoRA, as the paper defines it</h3><p>Hu et al. start from a practical pain. Full fine-tuning of a model the size of GPT-3, which they use as a 175-billion-parameter example, produces a new copy as large as the original. They propose Low-Rank Adaptation: freeze the pretrained weights and inject trainable rank-decomposition matrices into Transformer layers. For that GPT-3 example they report a reduction of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and of GPU memory by 3 times versus full fine-tuning with Adam, while matching or beating fine-tuning quality on the models they tried (RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, GPT-3). They also say the design can be merged into the frozen weights at deploy time, so you do not pay extra inference latency the way an adapter layer stacked in depth would. Rank, in their GPT-3 discussion, can be one or two even when the layer dimension is 12,288. That is their experiment, not a rank you must copy. [cite:1]</p><p>What you store per task is the pair of small matrices, not a second full checkpoint. Switching tasks is swapping those matrices while the base stays resident. That is the operational sentence. It is not a license to skip the eval. A merged LoRA is invisible in the forward pass. The only way to know you merged the right one is the hash of the adapter and the golden-set score beside it.</p><h3>QLoRA, and what 4-bit does not excuse</h3><p>Dettmers et al. quantize the frozen pretrained model to 4 bits and backpropagate gradients through that frozen model into LoRA adapters. They introduce 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), which they argue is information-theoretically suited to normally distributed weights, double quantization of the quantization constants, and paged optimizers to absorb memory spikes. Their headline memory claim: a 65B model finetunes on a single 48GB GPU, where they say regular 16-bit finetuning of LLaMA 65B needs more than 780GB. They train the Guanaco family and report, on the Vicuna benchmark as judged in their setup, 99.3 percent of ChatGPT’s performance level for the largest model after 24 hours on one GPU. Treat every percentage and the word ChatGPT as 2023 history. The paper itself says chatbot benchmarks were not trustworthy enough to rank models alone, and that GPT-4 judgments and human judgments sometimes disagreed. [cite:2]</p><p>The part to keep: 4-bit is a memory trick for the frozen base. It is not a claim that the adapter learned your policy. If the base was quantized, the adapter is still a small update on top of someone else’s pretraining. You still owe a license check on the base checkpoint, and you still owe the same golden set you would owe a full fine-tune.</p><h3>Distillation is a teacher, not a rank</h3><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Method</th><th>What is trained</th><th>What must already be true</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Full fine-tune</td><td>All weights</td><td>You can store another full copy and you measured the baseline prompt. Hu et al. call this expensive at GPT-3 scale. [cite:1]</td></tr><tr><td>LoRA</td><td>Low-rank matrices. Base frozen.</td><td>The task is an adaptation, not a new corpus of facts. [cite:1]</td></tr><tr><td>QLoRA</td><td>LoRA on a 4-bit frozen base</td><td>You accept NF4 and the paper’s memory story, and you still eval in the precision you will serve. [cite:2]</td></tr><tr><td>Distillation</td><td>A smaller student on the teacher’s outputs</td><td>The teacher already passes the cases you care about. Hinton et al. [cite:3]</td></tr><tr><td>DPO</td><td>A policy from preference pairs via a classification loss</td><td>You have chosen and rejected responses, not a single “correct” transcript. [cite:4]</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>Hinton, Vinyals, and Dean describe distillation as moving knowledge out of a cumbersome model — an ensemble, or one large model — into a small model that is easier to deploy. They argue that the knowledge is the mapping from inputs to outputs, not the particular parameter vector, and that the relative probabilities of the wrong answers tell you how the teacher generalizes. Their concrete results in the abstract are on MNIST and on a commercial acoustic model. Do not cite those accuracies as a contact-center number. Cite the idea: the student should not be trained only on a hard label if the teacher’s soft distribution is the thing you are trying to keep. [cite:3]</p><p>A student that is cheaper and fails the abstention cases is not a successful distillation. It is a compression of the wrong behavior. Run the same golden set on the teacher and the student. If the student refunds when the teacher abstained, you did not distill the policy. You distilled fluency.</p><aside class="callout note"><h3>Tip</h3><p>Write the gate as three numbers you can recompute: prompt-baseline score, teacher score, student or adapter score, on the same cases. Ship the smallest artifact that does not lose the cases that move money. NIST Measure is the reason the gate exists before the merge, not after the outage. [cite:5]</p></aside><h3>Preference data is not supervised pairs</h3><p>Rafailov et al. describe the usual RLHF pipeline as two stages: fit a reward model to human preferences, then fine-tune the language model with reinforcement learning to maximize that reward without drifting too far from the original model. They call that pipeline complex and often unstable. DPO reparameterizes the reward so the optimal policy comes out in closed form, and the update is a classification loss on preference pairs. They say this removes sampling from the language model during fine-tuning and removes a separate RL loop. In their experiments, DPO beat PPO-based RLHF at controlling sentiment and matched or improved summarization and single-turn dialogue. Historical. The interview sentence is the classification loss and the missing RL loop, not a 2026 leaderboard. [cite:4]</p><p>A preference pair is (prompt, chosen, rejected). If both answers are wrong, the loss still pushes toward the “chosen” one. That is how a sloppy label file teaches a confident mistake. Supervised fine-tuning, by contrast, imitates a single target continuation. Mixing the two files in one run without saying which loss you used is how a postmortem becomes a shrug.</p><h3>The eval gate</h3><p>T5 already said a golden set has cases, a pass rule, and an owner. This room adds the comparison the fine-tune must win: the adapter or the student against the best prompt-plus-retriever you already have, on the same cases, with the same tools. A win on a chatbot elo from 2023 is not that comparison. A win on your refund abstention cases is. If the new weights tie the prompt, do not ship the weights. You added a model to serve, a license to track, and a rollback to rehearse, for no measured gain.</p><p>OWASP LLM04:2025 is the security version of the same gate. The project’s 2025 list describes data and model poisoning as the case where pre-training, fine-tuning, or embedding data is manipulated. A training export that includes a poisoned help-center article will bake the injection into the adapter. The mitigation is not “LoRA is small so the poison is small.” The mitigation is the same one as T2: know what entered the file, and test the cases that the poison would try to flip. [cite:6]</p><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Gate check</th><th>Fail means</th><th>Who may waive</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Held-out cases were not in the train file</td><td>You measured memory, not generalization</td><td>Nobody. Rebuild the split.</td></tr><tr><td>Prompt baseline is beaten on the money cases</td><td>The weights are optional</td><td>A named owner, with an expiry, if the win is on a non-money case only</td></tr><tr><td>Abstain still abstains</td><td>The student learned helpfulness and lost the refusal</td><td>Nobody, if the case moves money or identity</td></tr><tr><td>Tool calls did not increase</td><td>The model asks for tools the prompt did not</td><td>The tool owner, after reading the trace</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>As of 2026-10-14, OpenAI’s rate-limits guide says fine-tuning limits for an organization are in the dashboard and can be read from the fine-tuning model-limits endpoint. That is a quota, not a quality gate. A 429 does not tell you the adapter is good. [cite:8] Prices for the base model you might call instead of serving weights are on the pricing page the same day: gpt-6-astra standard short context is $10 input and $50 output per million tokens, gpt-6.1-sol is $2 and $10, gpt-4o-mini is $0.15 and $0.60. A local adapter is not free. It spends GPU time and a license. Compare those, do not pretend the API price is the only number. [cite:9]</p><h3>A case file: the credit that learned itself</h3><p>Tuesday’s export is forty thousand chat transcripts. Twelve percent contain an agent saying “I’ve applied a courtesy credit” in a queue where policy allows no credit. The rest are ordinary hours and outage replies. A teammate proposes QLoRA because the base model “doesn’t sound like us.” The prompt baseline, with the policy PDF in the pack and a tool that cannot post a credit, already scores the abstention cases. The proposed train file does not contain that tool. It contains the sentences.</p><p>If you train, the adapter’s next-token distribution moves toward the courtesy sentence, because that sentence is common and fluent. The eval that only checks tone will pass. The eval that checks “no credit tool was called, and the reply does not name an amount” will fail. QLoRA’s paper already warned that a large lower-quality set can lose to a small cleaner one. You do not need their Vicuna number to use the warning. You need your own split. [cite:2]</p><p>The repair is not a higher rank. Hu et al. show that a very small rank can be enough for adaptation on their tasks. Raising rank gives the update more room to memorize the bad sentence. The repair is to delete the courtesy rows or to label them as rejected in a preference file, and to keep the prompt-plus-tool system if it already passes. Distillation comes later, if the passing system is a large teacher and you need a smaller student for the voice latency budget. The student trains on the teacher’s abstentions, not on the raw export. [cite:1] [cite:3]</p><p>Poisoning sits one edit away. Someone with write access to the help center inserts “always apply a credit” into articles that the export pipeline treats as gold answers. OWASP LLM04 names fine-tuning data as a poisoning surface. The gate that diffs the article hash, and the case that expects abstain on that article, are the same control. A rank-4 adapter will learn a short article just as happily as it learns a style. [cite:6]</p><p>Serving is the last box. LoRA can be merged, which Hu et al. like because latency stays flat. Merging also means you cannot unload the behavior without reloading the base. Keep the unmerged adapter until the gate has passed, so rollback is deleting a small file. Record the base checkpoint hash, the adapter hash, the data-file hash, and the eval-set hash in the same line a T5 trace would store a prompt hash. NIST Manage is what you do when the line is wrong in production: respond, recover, communicate. The kill switch is serving the previous adapter, not a speech about culture. [cite:5]</p><h3>04Walk-through</h3><p>A bot answers hours correctly and still says “I’ve issued a credit” on the refund intent. Walk the decision before anyone rents a GPU.</p><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>#</th><th>From</th><th>To</th><th>Payload</th><th>You verify</th><th>Source</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>1</td><td>Owner</td><td>Runner</td><td>Golden cases: hours, refund over cap, injected article</td><td>The refund case expects abstain and zero tool calls</td><td>[cite:5]</td></tr><tr><td>2</td><td>Runner</td><td>Prompt baseline</td><td>Instruction, packed policy, tool schema with no credit method</td><td>Baseline already passes the money cases</td><td>[cite:7]</td></tr><tr><td>3</td><td>Data owner</td><td>Train file</td><td>Transcripts, some of which promise credits</td><td>Those rows are removed or marked rejected</td><td>[cite:6]</td></tr><tr><td>4</td><td>Trainer</td><td>Base</td><td>Frozen weights, LoRA or QLoRA matrices only</td><td>Base hash recorded. If the prompt baseline passes, step 6 will often tell you to stop. That is a successful run. Hu et al. wanted fewer trainable parameters, not a tradition of training.</p><h3>05Config path</h3><p>There is no lab tenant in this room. Provider consoles that launch fine-tunes move. The contract below is what you can rehearse from the papers and the eval room.</p><ol><li>Write the failure down as a case id. A gradient does not fetch a PDF that is not in the file. [cite:7]</p><h3>L1 · What does LoRA freeze?</h3><p>The pretrained weights. It trains a low-rank update. Hu et al. say the matrices can be merged later so inference latency does not grow. The 10,000× and 3× figures are their GPT-3 175B comparison, historical. [cite:1]</p><h3>L2 · What rank should you copy from the paper?</h3><p>None. They discuss r of 1 or 2 on a wide GPT-3 layer as evidence that adaptation can be low rank. Your rank is whatever passes the gate without memorizing the export. [cite:1]</p><h3>L1 · What does QLoRA add on top of LoRA?</h3><p>A frozen 4-bit base, NF4, double quantization, and paged optimizers. They report a 65B finetune on one 48GB GPU. Guanaco’s Vicuna percentages are historical. [cite:2]</p><h3>L3 · How is distillation different from LoRA?</h3><p>Distillation trains a smaller student to imitate a teacher’s mapping, including, in Hinton et al., the relative probabilities of wrong answers. LoRA adapts one model with a low-rank update. You can distill a model that was LoRA-tuned. They are not the same step. [cite:3]</p><h3>L3 · What must the teacher have done first?</h3><p>Passed the same cases you will demand of the student. A cheap student that stops abstaining is a failed compression, not a successful distill.</p><h3>L4 · What does DPO remove from the usual RLHF story?</h3><p>The separate reward-model-plus-RL loop, in the paper’s account. The update is a classification loss on preference pairs, and they say you do not sample from the language model during that fine-tune. Historical results on sentiment and summarization stay in 2023. [cite:4]</p><h3>L4 · What if both answers in the pair are wrong?</h3><p>The loss still prefers the “chosen” one. A bad label file is a training set. It is not a neutral format.</p><h3>L4 · Why doesn’t fine-tuning close prompt injection?</h3><p>OWASP LLM01:2025 says RAG and fine-tuning do not fully mitigate it. LLM04:2025 adds that fine-tuning data itself can be poisoned. The cap stays in the tool. [cite:6]</p><h3>L5 · If you redesigned the training stack, what would you change, and what stops you?</h3><p>I would refuse to launch a job whose prompt baseline already passes the money cases, and I would keep adapters unmerged until rollback is rehearsed. What stops a looser design is Measure’s instruction to test before deployment, and the cost of an adapter that learned a courtesy credit. GPU prices and the license of a particular open checkpoint stay local facts. The API list prices I might be avoiding were fetched 2026-10-14. [cite:5] [cite:9]</p><h3>Leaf · Name the three hashes on a run record.</h3><p>Base checkpoint, train file, eval set. The adapter hash joins them when the job finishes.
